title: Reflection on Using GenAI
text: This page is a personal reflection on how I used a generative AI tool to help build this website. It will evolve as I use GenAI more across my modules.

title: Reflection on Using GenAI
text:
The Tool I Used
For this lab I used Claude (by Anthropic), accessed through the web chat interface at claude.ai. I chose it because it handles longer, multi-turn conversations well and is comfortable producing formatted text — Markdown, code chunks, file structures — which is exactly what a Quarto site needs.

title: Reflection on Using GenAI
text:
What I Used It For
I did not use Claude to write the website for me — I used it as a drafting partner. Specifically, it helped me:

Structure my homepage (index.qmd) — I gave it a few bullet points about myself (name, programme, hobbies, my dog Kimchi) and it shaped them into a coherent intro with proper Markdown formatting.
Generate placeholder templates for my project and data visualization pages, so I have a consistent structure to fill in later.
Explain Quarto-specific things — for example, the difference between source files (.qmd) and the auto-generated docs/ folder, and where to place an imgs/ directory so that Quarto picks it up correctly.
Apply Markdown patterns I had not used before, such as the float-left layout for putting an image of Kimchi beside text.

title: Reflection on Using GenAI
text:
What I Found Useful

Speed on boilerplate. Getting the scaffolding of a page — headings, lists, image syntax, code chunks — done in seconds meant I could focus on what I actually wanted to say.
Clear, focused explanations. When I asked a small technical question (where to put my imgs/ folder), I got a direct answer with the reasoning behind it, rather than having to dig through documentation.
Honest pushback when I gave too little. When I vaguely said I wanted to write about my “Week 2 Data Eng” assignment without giving any details, it didn’t invent a project — it asked me for the actual content. That mattered. It meant the output stayed grounded in things I’d actually done.

title: Reflection on Using GenAI
text:
What I Found Challenging
(Replace this with your own honest observations as you keep using GenAI. Some prompts to think about:)

Were there moments where the output felt generic or “AI-sounding,” and I had to rewrite it in my own voice?
Did I notice myself reaching for it too quickly, before thinking the problem through myself?
Were there places where its suggestions were confidently wrong, or technically off?

title: Reflection on Using GenAI
text:
What I Learned

GenAI is a multiplier, not a substitute. It can polish, structure, and format — but the substance has to come from me. When I had no project to write about, the best it could offer was an empty template.
The quality of the output tracks the quality of the input. Short, vague prompts gave short, generic results. When I gave more context (my year, my interests, my tone preference), the output got noticeably better.
Treat it as a draft, not a final answer. Everything it produced still needed a read-through, light edits, and personal touches before it felt like mine.

title: Reflection on Using GenAI
text:
Going Forward
In future modules I plan to:

Disclose where I used GenAI, the same way I’m doing on this page.
Avoid using it for anything I can’t explain or defend myself. If I can’t justify a line of code or a paragraph of writing on my own, it should not be in my submission.
Use it most where it helps me learn faster — explaining unfamiliar concepts, suggesting how to structure a piece of work, or catching mistakes — rather than as a way to skip the thinking.
